strengths: Clear problem formulation: Elegantly reframes diffusion caching as a Pareto multi-objective optimization problem, replacing hand-crafted heuristics with a principled approach

Strong and consistent empirical results: Achieves competitive or superior performance across multiple models (PixArt-α, PixArt-Σ, FLUX-1.dev) with comprehensive evaluation across metrics (Image Reward, FID, CLIP) and benchmarks (COCO, MJHQ-30K, PartiPrompts)

Impressive generalization properties: Schedules learned at 256×256 generalize to 1024×1024 without retraining; schedules transfer between model variants with minimal degradation—a notable advantage over hand-crafted methods like ToCa

Thorough experimental analysis: Extensive ablations on ECAD hyperparameters, calibration prompt sets, scaling properties, and comparison with concurrent work (DuCa); clear visualization of learned schedules

Practical applicability: Requires no model parameter modifications, low memory footprint, asynchronous optimization capability, applicable to off-the-shelf models, reproducibility through promised code release
Well-structured presentation: Comprehensive appendix with detailed methods, additional results, proper ablations, and informative visualizations of learned caching patterns across models
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: Core contribution is applying standard NSGA-II multi-objective optimization to diffusion caching—primarily domain application rather than algorithmic innovation; no comparison with alternative optimization approaches (Bayesian optimization, RL, other multi-objective methods)

Substantial and incompletely analyzed optimization cost: PixArt-α requires 39.6M image generations (550 gen × 72 schedules × 1,000 images), FLUX-1.dev requires 6M; no wall-clock time provided; no cost-benefit analysis comparing total compute (optimization + inference) vs. training-based acceleration methods

Metric dependency and limited metric independence: Entire optimization pipeline depends on Image Reward chosen for 'cost and time'; circular reasoning obscures lack of multi-metric optimization; while FID and CLIP evaluated post-hoc, they were not part of optimization objective; calibration set affects results (Table 8: MJHQ FID varies 19.54-26.66); no human evaluation despite claims

Limited interpretability and theoretical understanding: Visualizations of learned schedules lack analysis of why specific patterns emerge; unclear what makes certain timesteps/blocks critical or why similar patterns appear across different architectures; no feature importance analysis or component ablations

Incomplete experimental comparisons: ToCa comparison uses normalized latencies due to implementation differences, complicating direct comparison; FLUX-1.dev ToCa results optimized at different resolutions; DuCa comparison relegated to appendix; MAC-to-latency correlation acknowledged but not deeply analyzed

Calibration set sensitivity and unclear generalization: Table 8 shows dependence on calibration prompts; Image Reward-calibrated schedule significantly outperforms DrawBench200-calibrated (MJHQ FID 19.54 vs 26.66); no principled guidance on calibration set size/diversity requirements; generalization to different downstream domains unclear

strengths: Clear and principled problem formulation: Reformulating caching as multi-objective Pareto optimization is elegant and enables fine-grained quality-latency tradeoffs
Practical no-modification approach requiring no gradients, weight updates, or model retraining, with lower memory overhead than training-based alternatives
Strong empirical results: 2.58× speedup on FLUX.1-dev while maintaining/exceeding baseline quality; consistent improvements across PixArt-α, PixArt-Σ, and FLUX.1-dev
Excellent generalization: Schedules transfer to unseen model variants (PixArt-α→PixArt-Σ) and resolutions (256×256→1024×1024) with minimal degradation
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple metrics (FID, CLIP, Image Reward) and benchmarks (COCO, MJHQ-30k, PartiPrompts) with comparisons to recent baselines
Thorough ablation studies: Hyperparameters, initialization strategies, calibration selection, metric alternatives, and inference steps all systematically evaluated
Flexible, general framework: Component selection, quality metrics, and calibration sources are customizable; applicability beyond text-to-image claimed
High reproducibility standards: Promises code release, detailed algorithm specification, clear hyperparameters, and extensive implementation details in appendix
weaknesses: Substantial up-front optimization cost (~700 A6000 GPU-hours for full frontier, 44 GPU-hours minimum) with insufficient guidance on compute-quality tradeoffs, limiting accessibility for practitioners with constrained resources

Limited algorithmic novelty: Core contribution applies standard NSGA-II (2013) to straightforward binary optimization; main innovation is problem reformulation rather than methodology, with no exploration of alternative multi-objective optimizers

Metric dependence: All primary results optimized for Image Reward without sufficient validation of its correlation with human preferences for accelerated models; ablation shows CLIP-based metrics yield 16% worse speedups
Incomplete concurrent work comparison: SpeCa and ClusCa relegated to appendix despite appearing to be important related methods; dismissal of 50-step comparisons lacks justification

Limited interpretability: Learned schedules shown as heatmaps but with minimal analysis of design principles, pattern emergence, or why genetic algorithm solutions work—missed opportunity for insights
Incomplete generalization analysis: While transfer results are shown, formal bounds on generalization are missing; sensitivity to model architecture changes unexplored
Latency measurement inconsistencies: Different baseline implementations across methods with normalization procedure introducing uncertainty; would benefit from unified implementation
Calibration set sensitivity: Although ablations provided, guidance for practitioners on calibration set size for new domains/models is limited; significant degradation with only 10 prompts
Presentation issues: 39-page appendix makes navigation difficult; important details (concurrent work, calibration ablations) relegated to appendix; some figures small and hard to read
Missing failure analysis: Predominantly positive results with limited discussion of failure cases, performance outside tested settings, or robustness to architecture variations

strengths: Clear problem formulation as Pareto multi-objective optimization with strong motivation for moving away from hand-crafted heuristics
Exceptionally comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple models (PixArt-α, PixArt-Σ, FLUX.1-dev), datasets, and metrics; extensive ablations in appendix
Demonstrated generalization across model variants and resolutions, with practical value for practitioners
Strong empirical results consistently beating or matching recent baselines (FORA, ToCa, DuCa, TaylorSeer) across all settings
Non-invasive approach requiring no weight modifications; excellent reproducibility with thorough documentation and promised code release
Smooth Pareto frontier discovery rather than discrete operating points enables fine-grained quality-latency tradeoffs
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: core contribution is applying standard NSGA-II (2013) to binary mask optimization; no novel algorithm components, theoretical insights, or principled justification for genetic algorithms over alternatives (Bayesian optimization, gradient-based methods, evolutionary strategies)

Expensive search phase (44-700 GPU-hours) inadequately disclosed in main paper and undermines 'efficiency' claims; misleading 'training-free' framing (should be 'weight-update-free'); each model variant requires 50+ additional generations

Entire approach dependent on Image Reward as optimization metric; this learned model has own biases/limitations; different metrics yield different Pareto frontiers (Table 6); method is only as good as the metric used

Incomplete baseline comparisons: latencies normalized due to implementation differences; TaylorSeer batch size reduced 66% for memory reasons; unclear how much improvement is from ECAD vs. better implementation
Lack of interpretability: no analysis of why learned patterns emerge (Figure 5); what makes schedules 'good'?; why are early/late steps differently cacheable?; schedules visualized but not explained

Overstated generalization: transfer to PixArt-Σ requires 50 generations of optimization (not zero-shot); resolution transfer shows quality drops; no theoretical understanding of why generalization occurs

Calibration set still substantial (100 prompts × 10 images = 1000 calibration generations); performance degrades significantly with fewer prompts (33 prompts: FID 8.18→10.02); generation cost not included in reported GPU-hours

Hyperparameter sensitivity of ECAD itself: population size, mutation rate, crossover points vary results (Table 9); how were ECAD hyperparameters selected? No ablation on NSGA-II components vs. simpler search
Modest practical improvements: PixArt-α 1.97× vs. ToCa 1.83× (8% gain); FLUX 2.58× vs. FORA 2.44× (6% gain); insufficient ROI for 44-700 GPU-hours of search
Limited scope: only text-to-image generation demonstrated; only DiTs tested; only 20-step inference; claims of generality unproven; doesn't address other acceleration techniques

Missing ablations: no comparison with random search over binary masks; no justification for NSGA-II over other multi-objective optimizers (MOEA/D, etc.); no analysis of contribution of good initialization (Figure 13) vs. optimization
Stochastic algorithm variance not quantified; no reporting of runs across random seeds; reproducibility limited until code release

strengths: Novel problem formulation: Reframes diffusion caching as multi-objective Pareto optimization, providing a principled alternative to hand-crafted heuristics

Strong empirical results: 4.47 COCO FID improvement over SOTA on PixArt-α while increasing speedup from 2.35x to 2.58x; consistent gains across PixArt-α/Σ and FLUX.1-dev on multiple metrics (FID, CLIP, Image Reward)
Impressive generalization: Schedules transfer effectively across model variants (PixArt-α→Σ) and resolutions (256×256→1024×1024) without retraining, a clear advantage over prior heuristic methods
Comprehensive evaluation: Rigorous ablations on population size, images/prompt, calibration set diversity, NSGA-II hyperparameters, and metric choice; thorough baseline comparisons across 3 datasets
Practical advantages: No weight updates, lower memory than distillation, asynchronous operation, modular framework, fine-grained quality-latency control via Pareto frontiers
Reproducibility: Clear algorithm description, detailed hyperparameters, extensive appendix (47 pages) with visualizations and implementation details, code promised to be released
weaknesses: Substantial optimization cost: Full Pareto frontier requires ~700 GPU-hours; competitive schedules need 44-145 GPU-hours, though framed as one-time cost, no concrete wall-clock improvements with engineered implementations provided
Metric dependence: Schedules optimized primarily for Image Reward; Appendix A.3 shows CLIP-based alternatives underperform; lack of human evaluation studies weakens quality claims
Limited algorithmic novelty: Uses standard NSGA-II (Deb & Jain 2013) with straightforward binary mask representation; conceptual contribution (problem reformulation) is primary strength

Shallow mechanistic analysis: Learned schedule patterns are visualized but not deeply interpreted; why certain structures emerge (e.g., cross-attention cacheability in late steps) lacks investigation; limited insights into principles guiding evolution
Calibration set requirements: Requires 100 diverse prompts; Table 8 shows 10-prompt performance degrades substantially; reduces applicability in new domains or few-shot scenarios

Limited experimental scope: Only evaluated on text-to-image with 20 steps; claims about 'class-conditioned or text-to-video tasks' are unsupported; 3 models all from similar DiT architecture families; inference step transfer uses simple up/downscaling

Comparison methodology: Latency normalization required due to different baseline implementations (Appendix A.11); confounding factors (TaylorSeer batch size constraints); could benefit from independent re-implementation
Incomplete analysis: Limited discussion of what drives differences in Pareto frontiers across models (Figure 14-15), why schedules change dramatically across generations (Figure 23), or failure modes
